_readme: SAIRNlaw deadline engine seed -- STATE appellate deadlines. Phase 8c.
Ohio, Indiana, Michigan and Pennsylvania. Every value read from primary
source 2026-08-23 and quoted in the row.
Until now 'appellate' was a federal-only domain -- three FRAP rules and
nothing else. Every state carried civil-litigation rules only, so a user
who selected a state and the appellate domain got an honest refusal and no
coverage. That is what this file closes.
NO NEW ENGINE CAPABILITY WAS NEEDED. Every shape these rules use already
exists: single trigger, later_of and earlier_of multi-trigger, and the
retrigger that REPLACES a trigger without adding days. That the four states'
appellate rules decompose cleanly into shapes built for federal rules in
Phases 1-2 is worth recording -- it is the third phase running where the
capability turned out to fit rules it was not built against.
FOUR STATES, FOUR DIFFERENT DAY COUNTS, AND THE SHORTEST ONE IS THE TRAP:
Ohio          30 days   App.R. 4(A)(1)
Indiana       30 days   App.R. 9(A)(1)
Michigan      21 days   MCR 7.204(A)(1)
Pennsylvania  30 days   Pa.R.A.P. 903(a), BUT 10 days under 903(c)(1)
Michigan's 21 days is nine days shorter than its neighbours' and its own
case law treats timeliness as jurisdictional. Pennsylvania's 10-day
provision is shorter still and applies only to three named subject matters.
A practitioner carrying a 30-day habit across a state line loses the appeal,
which is why each state is seeded with its own count and its own citation
rather than a shared appellate rule.
OHIO'S LATE-SERVICE PROVISION IS A DIFFERENT TRIGGER, NOT A LATER-OF. App.R.
4(A)(3) reads: 'if the clerk has not completed service of notice of the
judgment within the three-day period prescribed in Civ.R. 58(B), the 30-day
periods referenced in App.R. 4(A)(1) and 4(A)(2) BEGIN TO RUN on the date
when the clerk actually completes service.' The period does not run from the
later of two events -- it runs from entry normally, and from actual service
instead when service was late. Two distinct triggers, because whether the
clerk served within three days is a case fact the engine has no field for.
OHIO'S POST-JUDGMENT TOLLING IS THE RETRIGGER SHAPE, unchanged from FRAP
4(a)(4)(A): 'the time for filing a notice of appeal ... begins to run as to
all parties when the trial court enters an order resolving the LAST of these
post-judgment filings.' Six qualifying filings are listed and encoded. As
with the federal rule, this REPLACES the trigger and adds no days, and a
qualifying filing recorded as pending with no disposition returns
MOTION_PENDING rather than a guessed date.
INDIANA'S MOTION-TO-CORRECT-ERROR BRANCH IS AN EARLIER_OF, and it is only
the second one in the whole engine. App.R. 9(A)(1): thirty days after the
ruling is noted in the Chronological Case Summary 'or thirty (30) days after
the motion is deemed denied under Trial Rule 53.3, WHICHEVER OCCURS FIRST.'
Both limbs carry the same thirty-day count, so the existing earlier_of
resolution expresses it exactly. Note the consequence Indiana attaches:
App.R. 9(A)(5), 'Unless the Notice of Appeal is timely filed, the right to
appeal shall be forfeited' -- carried in the rule labels.
MICHIGAN HAS FOUR ALTERNATIVE TRIGGERS FOR ONE PERIOD. MCR 7.204(A)(1)(a)
through (d) each start the same 21 days from a different event. Seeded as
four rules with four triggers, the same treatment MCR 2.108(A)'s splits get.
TWO OF THEM CARRY CONDITIONS THE ENGINE CANNOT CHECK and both are disclosed
in their rows: (c) applies only if the trial court received the request
within the initial 21-day period, and (d) only if the post-judgment motion
was filed within that period or within further time the court allowed for
good cause. The engine computes from the event it is given and does not
verify the condition was met.
PENNSYLVANIA'S TEN-DAY PROVISION IS SEEDED AS THREE RULES, NOT ONE. Pa.R.A.P.
903(c)(1) applies a ten-day period to three unrelated subject matters --
venue or venire in a criminal proceeding, matters under the Election Code,
and matters under the Local Government Unit Debt Act. Which one applies is a
fact about the case, so collapsing them into a single trigger would make the
engine guess. Each gets its own trigger and its own row quoting its own limb.
TWO RULES DELIBERATELY NOT SEEDED, both because a limb is a COMPUTED PERIOD
rather than an event date -- the same reason FRCP 15(a)(3) was refused in
Phase 5:
Ohio App.R. 4(B)(1) cross-appeal: another party may file 'within the
appeal time period otherwise prescribed by this rule OR within ten days of
the filing of the first notice of appeal.' The first limb is whatever this
rule would otherwise compute, not a date anyone supplies. Encoding it as a
later_of would silently drop that limb and produce ten days from the first
notice in every case -- too early whenever the original period had longer
to run. Pennsylvania's cross-appeal rule has no such problem and IS seeded:
Pa.R.A.P. 903(b) runs a flat fourteen days from service of the first notice.
Pa.R.A.P. 903(c)(2) and 903(c)(3): (c)(2) runs from the filing of an
election under Rule 311(b) and (c)(3) from imposition of sentence in open
court where no post-sentence motion was filed. Both are readable, but
neither was verified to the standard applied to the rest of this file, and
the conditions attached to (c)(3) were not read in full. Absence means not
yet verified, not verified absent.
NO SERVICE EXTENSION on any rule here. Appellate periods in these four states
run from entry, from a docket notation, or from a court's own order, not
from being served with a paper, so the condition FRCP 6(d) and its state
analogues state is not met. Ohio's App.R. 4(A)(3) is the closest thing to a
service-linked provision and it moves the TRIGGER rather than adding days.

rules.label: Notice of appeal from an order final upon its entry (Ohio)

trigger_document.label: the date the clerk ENTERED the order or judgment on the docket
trigger_document.not_the: the date it was signed, decided, announced in court, or mailed to the parties -- those are different events and they bear different dates

authority.quote: Subject to the provisions of App.R. 4(A)(3), a party who wishes to appeal from an order that is final upon its entry shall file the notice of appeal required by App.R. 3 within 30 days of that entry.
authority.note: The retrigger implements App.R. 4(B)(2): where a qualifying post-judgment filing is made, 'the time for filing a notice of appeal from the judgment or final order in question begins to run as to all parties when the trial court enters an order resolving the LAST of these post-judgment filings.' That REPLACES the trigger and adds no days, identical in shape to FRAP 4(a)(4)(A). A qualifying filing recorded as pending with no disposition returns MOTION_PENDING rather than a guessed date. Use the separate 4(A)(3) rule instead if the clerk did not complete service within Civ.R. 58(B)'s three days.

rules.label: Notice of appeal where the clerk served notice late — runs from actual service (Ohio)

authority.quote: In a civil case, if the clerk has not completed service of notice of the judgment within the three-day period prescribed in Civ.R. 58(B), the 30-day periods referenced in App.R. 4(A)(1) and 4(A)(2) begin to run on the date when the clerk actually completes service.
authority.note: A DIFFERENT TRIGGER, not a later-of. The rule says the period BEGINS TO RUN on the date of actual service, so where service was late the period runs from that date instead of from entry -- not from whichever is later. Whether the clerk served within three days is a case fact the engine has no field for, so this is a distinct trigger the caller selects rather than a condition the engine evaluates. Same 30 days as 4(A)(1).

rules.label: Notice of appeal from a Final Judgment (Indiana — untimely filing FORFEITS the right to appeal)

trigger_document.label: the date the entry of final judgment was NOTED IN THE CHRONOLOGICAL CASE SUMMARY
trigger_document.not_the: the date the judgment was signed, or the date it was mailed -- Ind. App. R. 9(A)(1) keys on the CCS notation specifically

authority.quote: thirty (30) days after the entry of a Final Judgment is noted in the Chronological Case Summary
authority.note: THE TRIGGER IS THE DOCKET NOTATION, not the judgment itself -- the period runs from when entry is noted in the Chronological Case Summary, which can differ from the date the judgment was signed. Indiana attaches a hard consequence: App.R. 9(A)(5), 'Unless the Notice of Appeal is timely filed, the right to appeal shall be forfeited except as provided by P.C.R. 2.' That is carried in the rule label. Use the separate motion-to-correct-error rule instead if a timely such motion was filed.

rules.label: Notice of appeal after a timely motion to correct error — earlier of ruling or deemed denial (Indiana)

authority.quote: if any party files a timely motion to correct error, a Notice of Appeal must be filed within thirty (30) days after the court's ruling on such motion is noted in the Chronological Case Summary or thirty (30) days after the motion is deemed denied under Trial Rule 53.3, whichever occurs first
authority.note: ONLY THE SECOND earlier_of RULE IN THE ENGINE, after FRCP 15(a)(1)(B). Both limbs carry the same thirty-day count, so the existing earlier_of resolution expresses the rule exactly. The refusal direction matters here as it does everywhere earlier_of appears: resolving from a partial set produces a date that is too LATE, which is the direction that forfeits the appeal under App.R. 9(A)(5). The engine refuses with INCOMPLETE_TRIGGERS and names which date is missing rather than computing from the one supplied.

rules.label: Claim of appeal from the judgment or order appealed from (Michigan — 21 days, jurisdictional)

trigger_document.label: the date the clerk ENTERED the order or judgment on the docket
trigger_document.not_the: the date it was signed, decided, announced in court, or mailed to the parties -- those are different events and they bear different dates

authority.quote: the judgment or order appealed from
authority.note: TWENTY-ONE DAYS, NINE FEWER THAN EVERY NEIGHBOURING STATE IN THIS ENGINE. Ohio, Indiana and Pennsylvania all allow thirty for the ordinary civil appeal; Michigan allows twenty-one, and Michigan case law treats appellate timeliness as jurisdictional with no extensions. A practitioner carrying a thirty-day habit across the state line loses the appeal, which is the single most consequential divergence in this file. MCR 7.204(A)(1) provides four alternative triggers for this same 21-day period; this is the ordinary one.

rules.label: Claim of appeal running from an order appointing counsel (Michigan)

trigger_document.label: the date the clerk ENTERED the order or judgment on the docket
trigger_document.not_the: the date it was signed, decided, announced in court, or mailed to the parties -- those are different events and they bear different dates

authority.note: One of four alternative triggers for the same 21-day period under MCR 7.204(A)(1). Seeded as its own rule with its own trigger because which event started the clock is a case fact, and four rules sharing one trigger name would be refused as AMBIGUOUS_RULE rather than chosen between.

rules.label: Claim of appeal running from denial of a request for appointed counsel (Michigan)

trigger_document.label: the date the clerk ENTERED the order or judgment on the docket
trigger_document.not_the: the date it was signed, decided, announced in court, or mailed to the parties -- those are different events and they bear different dates

authority.quote: an order denying a request for appointment of counsel in a civil case in which an indigent party is entitled to appointed counsel, if the trial court received the request within the initial 21-day appeal period
authority.note: A CONDITION THE ENGINE CANNOT CHECK, disclosed rather than ignored: this trigger applies only if the trial court received the request within the initial 21-day appeal period, and only in a civil case where an indigent party is entitled to appointed counsel. The engine computes 21 days from the denial order it is given and does NOT verify either condition was met. If the request was late, this rule does not apply at all and the date produced would be meaningless.

rules.label: Claim of appeal running from an order deciding a post-judgment motion (Michigan)

trigger_document.label: the date the clerk ENTERED the order or judgment on the docket
trigger_document.not_the: the date it was signed, decided, announced in court, or mailed to the parties -- those are different events and they bear different dates

authority.quote: an order deciding a postjudgment motion for new trial, rehearing, reconsideration, or other relief from the order or judgment appealed, if the motion was filed within the initial 21-day appeal period or within any further time that the trial court has allowed for good cause during that 21-day period
authority.note: A CONDITION THE ENGINE CANNOT CHECK, disclosed: this trigger applies only if the post-judgment motion was filed within the initial 21-day appeal period, or within further time the trial court allowed for good cause during that period. The engine computes from the deciding order it is given and does not verify the motion was timely. Note this is a SEPARATE TRIGGER rather than a retrigger clause, unlike Ohio App.R. 4(B)(2) and FRAP 4(a)(4)(A) -- Michigan's rule lists it as one of four alternative starting events rather than as a substitution applied to the ordinary period, and it is encoded the way its own rule states it.

trigger_document.label: the date the clerk ENTERED the order or judgment on the docket
trigger_document.not_the: the date it was signed, decided, announced in court, or mailed to the parties -- those are different events and they bear different dates

authority.quote: the notice of appeal required by Rule 902 (manner of taking appeal) shall be filed within 30 days after the entry of the order from which the appeal is taken
authority.note: The ordinary Pennsylvania appeal period. BUT SEE the three ten-day rules also seeded here under Pa.R.A.P. 903(c)(1) -- venue or venire in a criminal proceeding, Election Code matters, and Local Government Unit Debt Act matters each run ten days, not thirty. Computed under Pa.R.J.A. 107, and effective_from is 2024-01-01 for the same reason as every Pennsylvania rule in this engine: that is when Pa.R.J.A. 107 took effect and Pa.R.C.P. 106 was rescinded, and this row is the pairing of the count with a computation standard.

rules.label: Cross appeal after another party's notice of appeal (Pennsylvania)

authority.quote: if a timely notice of appeal is filed by a party, any other party may file a notice of appeal within 14 days of the date on which the first notice of appeal was served
authority.note: SEEDED WHERE OHIO'S CROSS-APPEAL RULE COULD NOT BE, and the difference is instructive. Pennsylvania runs a flat fourteen days from a single event -- service of the first notice -- which is directly computable. Ohio App.R. 4(B)(1) instead allows the later of 'the appeal time period otherwise prescribed by this rule' or ten days from the first notice, and that first limb is a computed period rather than an event date, so it is refused rather than approximated. Same rule family, different shapes, different outcomes.

rules.label: Notice of appeal from an order changing venue or venire in a criminal proceeding (Pennsylvania — 10 days)

trigger_document.label: the date the clerk ENTERED the order or judgment on the docket
trigger_document.not_the: the date it was signed, decided, announced in court, or mailed to the parties -- those are different events and they bear different dates

authority.quote: An order changing venue or venire in a criminal proceeding
authority.note: TEN DAYS, NOT THIRTY -- a third of the ordinary Pennsylvania period, and the shortest appellate deadline anywhere in this engine. Rule 903(c)(1) applies the same ten days to three unrelated subject matters; each is seeded as its own rule with its own trigger, because which one applies is a fact about the case and collapsing them would make the engine guess. Ten days is short enough that the computation standard matters: Pa.R.J.A. 107 has no short-period exclusion, so intermediate weekends and holidays are counted and only the last day rolls.

rules.label: Notice of appeal in a matter arising under the Pennsylvania Election Code (Pennsylvania — 10 days)

trigger_document.label: the date the clerk ENTERED the order or judgment on the docket
trigger_document.not_the: the date it was signed, decided, announced in court, or mailed to the parties -- those are different events and they bear different dates

authority.quote: An order in any matter arising under the Pennsylvania Election Code
authority.note: Ten days rather than the ordinary thirty. Distinct trigger from the other two subject matters sharing Rule 903(c)(1), so the engine never guesses which limb applies. Note that Pennsylvania's own holiday calendar includes Election Day itself as a legal holiday under 44 P.S. Sec. 11 -- a ten-day period in an election matter can therefore land on a day the statute makes a holiday, and the engine rolls it.

rules.label: Notice of appeal in a matter arising under the Local Government Unit Debt Act (Pennsylvania — 10 days)

trigger_document.label: the date the clerk ENTERED the order or judgment on the docket
trigger_document.not_the: the date it was signed, decided, announced in court, or mailed to the parties -- those are different events and they bear different dates

authority.quote: An order in any matter arising under the Local Government Unit Debt Act or any similar statute
authority.note: Ten days rather than thirty. The rule's own words extend this to 'any similar statute', which the engine cannot evaluate -- whether another statute is similar enough is a legal judgment, not a computation. This row covers the Local Government Unit Debt Act itself; a matter under a statute a practitioner believes similar should be checked by hand rather than assumed covered here.

rules.label: Notice of appeal by another party after a timely first notice of appeal, the later of the ordinary period and ten days (Ohio)

limbs.label: 30 days after entry of the final order, the App.R. 4(A)(1) period
10 days after the first notice of appeal was filed

authority.quote: If a notice of appeal is timely filed by a party, another party may file a notice of appeal within the appeal time period otherwise prescribed by this rule or within ten days of the filing of the first notice of appeal.
authority.note: NOW COMPUTABLE. This rule was refused by this engine until 2026-08-24 because its two limbs carry DIFFERENT counts -- 30 days from entry, 10 days from the first notice of appeal -- and the older multi-trigger shape resolved between trigger DATES under a single shared count. resolve_periods computes each limb in full and compares the results. NOTE THE RULE SAYS "or", NOT "whichever is later". A widely repeated secondary paraphrase supplies "whichever is later"; those words are NOT in App.R. 4(B)(1) and are not quoted above. The later-of reading follows from the structure -- it is a permission listing two alternatives, and an appellee who may act within either has until the later expires -- but it is a reading, not the rule's language, and it is recorded as such. LIMB ONE ASSUMES App.R. 4(A)(1). Where App.R. 4(A)(2) applies (an order not final upon entry) or App.R. 4(A)(3) applies (the clerk did not complete service within the three-day Civ.R. 58(B) period, so the 30 days run from actual service instead), the first limb runs from a DIFFERENT event and this row is wrong. Ohio already carries a separate 4(A)(3) row for the ordinary appeal; no 4(B)(1) variant is seeded for it, and that is an explicit decision rather than an oversight -- which of the three 4(A) limbs governs is a case fact the engine has no field for.
